---
title: "Reproducibility repositories"
subtitle: "Dataverse, Zenodo, the code forges and the Open Science Framework"
bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib]
---



This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) is about where a finished piece of research is deposited, so that another person can find it, cite it and run it again. It sets out what a repository has to do, compares the repositories that researchers actually use, and then follows the public record of the housing-audit case through them. That record is unusually complete. The original authors (OAs) deposited their data and code on the Harvard Dataverse when their paper appeared [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect], the SCORE programme kept everything that it did with the paper in one tree of projects on the Open Science Framework (OSF) [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen], and the five Multi100 analysts left their scripts there too [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. Reading that record is an exercise in itself, and the module ends with one, followed by a route for depositing a reanalysis of your own. Section 7 sets the record of the EU-frames case beside it, a dossier in which SCORE carried out all three of its activities and which is held on the OSF in the same way, and section 8 explains what the transition of the OSF at the end of 2026 means for both.

The module assumes no more than the course itself does. It is a natural companion to the [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd), which is about keeping a history of your own work and collaborating on it. The two overlap at GitHub, which is both a working tool and a place where code is found.

## 1. What a repository does {#sec-what}

A folder on a laptop, a departmental server and a link in the appendix of a paper share a weakness: none of them outlasts the person who made it. A repository in the sense meant here does six things that those do not, and the six serve as a checklist for choosing one.

- **A persistent identifier.** A DOI (digital object identifier) or an equivalent that resolves to the deposit for as long as the repository exists, and that a paper can cite. Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare and the OSF all mint DOIs, and a GitHub repository does not.
- **Versioning.** A new version gets a new identifier or a new version number while the old one still resolves, so that a reader who follows the citation in a paper gets what the paper used.
- **A licence.** A statement, attached to the deposit, of what others may do with it. CC BY 4.0 is the common choice for text and figures, CC0 for data that the depositor places in the public domain, and an open-source licence such as MIT for code. The licence of the underlying data limits what you may deposit at all.
- **Metadata.** A title, creators, a description, keywords, related identifiers and dates, in a form that indexes and catalogues can read. The quality of the metadata decides whether anyone who was not sent the link ever finds the deposit.
- **Preservation.** A commitment, usually institutional, to keep the files readable over decades, sometimes certified (the CoreTrustSeal is the certification that most social-science archives hold).
- **Access control.** Public by default, with the possibility of an embargo, a restricted file for which a reader applies, or a private deposit that only a reviewer can reach through a link.

Repositories come in four kinds, and the guidance that the Center for Open Science (COS) wrote for researchers moving off OSF projects sorts them in the same way: archives for a discipline (the UK Data Service, GESIS, ICPSR, the Qualitative Data Repository), generalist repositories (Zenodo, Figshare, Dataverse, Dryad), the repositories that universities run for their own staff, and repositories attached to a journal or a publisher. The same guidance recommends a first step: "Talk to your institutional librarian about who should host your data and other research outputs." Funders and journals increasingly require a named repository, and the housing-audit case shows a journal that keeps a collection of its own: the package of the OAs sits in the collection of the *American Journal of Political Science* on the Harvard Dataverse.

## 2. The generalist repositories {#sec-generalist}

| Repository | What it takes | Identifier and versions | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/)** | Any research output: data, code, materials, slides, reports | A DOI per version and a concept DOI for all versions | Free, hosted by CERN | Records can be linked to one another as parts of a whole; a GitHub repository can be set to archive each release automatically, which is the standard way of giving code a DOI |
| **[Harvard Dataverse](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/)** and the other Dataverse installations | Datasets with their documentation; collections nest, so a journal or a project can be a collection with datasets inside it | A DOI per dataset, with numbered versions | Free at Harvard; institutional installations elsewhere | Embargo and restricted access by file; the `dataverse` R package uploads and downloads by DOI |
| **[Figshare](https://figshare.com/)** | Datasets, code, figures, presentations, posters | A DOI per item and version | Free for individuals; many universities run their own instance | Quick to use; the instances run by universities are often the university repository under another name |
| **[Dryad](https://datadryad.org/)** | Data accompanying a journal article, curated | A DOI | A charge for publishing the data, often paid by the journal or the institution | Curation is what you pay for |
| **[UK Data Service ReShare](https://reshare.ukdataservice.ac.uk/)** | Research data from UK projects, in particular those funded by the ESRC | A persistent identifier and a catalogue record | Free | The route that satisfies the data policy of the ESRC; the data join the national collection and take on its tiers of access |
| **ICPSR (openICPSR)** | Social and behavioural science data, deposited by the researcher or curated | A DOI | Deposit by the researcher free; curation priced | The US counterpart of ReShare |
| **[Qualitative Data Repository](https://qdr.syr.edu/)** | Qualitative and multi-method data, with curators who help depositors share sensitive data ethically and legally | A DOI | Typical deposit fees of $750 to $2,500, as quoted by COS; often waived at member institutions | Specialised in interview and fieldwork data |
| **The Open Science Framework** | Registrations and preprints; until February 2027, projects holding anything | A DOI for public registrations and, on request, for projects | Free | See [section 7](#sec-osf) |

The rows are drawn from the guide that COS published on [choosing a repository](https://help.osf.io/article/735-choosing-a-repository), read on 8 September 2026, and from the pages of the repositories themselves. Which one to use depends on what the deposit is. A dataset that other people should find and reuse goes to the archive of its discipline if there is one and to Dataverse or Zenodo otherwise. Code goes to a forge (the next section), with each release archived on Zenodo. A finished report, a set of slides or a preprint goes to Zenodo or Figshare, or to the preprint server of your field.

## 3. Code forges {#sec-forges}

[GitHub](https://github.com/), [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/), [Codeberg](https://codeberg.org/) and the self-hosted Forgejo are *forges*: services that host git repositories with an issue tracker, pull requests and, in the case of GitHub and GitLab, a great deal else, from automated builds to website hosting. They are where code is written, reviewed and shared, and the [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd) is about using them for that. They are also where most research code is found, which makes them look like repositories in the sense of this page, but they lack the properties listed in section 1. A GitHub repository has no DOI, its owner can rename, transfer or delete it in a minute, and it comes with no commitment to preservation. The remedy is cheap and standard: tag a release on the forge and let Zenodo archive it, which gives the release a DOI that a paper can cite while the forge keeps the working copy. The workspace of each case is maintained in a GitHub repository of its own, [{{< var cases.housing.template-repo >}}]({{< var cases.housing.template-repo >}}) for the housing-audit case and [{{< var template-repo >}}]({{< var template-repo >}}) for the EU-frames case, and the same remedy applies to them.

## 4. The package of the housing-audit study {#sec-dataverse}

The OAs deposited their replication package in the collection of the *American Journal of Political Science* on the Harvard Dataverse, under the title "Replication Data for: Does Race Affect Access to Government Services? An Experiment Exploring Street-Level Bureaucrats and Access to Public Housing", at [doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU). It holds six files. The data file was deposited in the format of Stata, and Dataverse also offers it as tabular text, a form that any program can read. Beside it are two Stata do-files, one that runs the analyses on the public data and one that runs them on the identifiable data used in the paper, a codebook for each of the two data files, and a ReadMe that explains how the files fit together. The identifiable data file itself is not in the package, so its do-file and codebook document an analysis that no reader can run.

**The licence.** The package is released under CC0, which places the files in the public domain, so that anyone may copy, change and redistribute them without asking. The terms field reads "This dataset is made available under a Creative Commons CC0 license with the following additional/modified terms and conditions:", with nothing after it. The course relies on that dedication when it commits the data file and every file derived from it, and when this site serves them.

**The blinding.** The ReadMe explains why the public file differs from the file of the paper. The census codes that matched each housing authority to its community "would reveal the identities of the housing authorities / officials in the data", and the continuous values of the community characteristics "also uniquely identify the observations". The ReadMe gives the reason why that matters: "Whether or not a housing official responded, particularly to an ostensible minority applicant, is very sensitive and potentially harmful information." The OAs therefore replaced population, percent white, Black and Hispanic, the poverty rate and the HUD assessment score with thirds of their distributions, lower, middle and top. The ReadMe states the consequence: the public data "will enable public replication of some results in full (the experimental results that do not require demographic variables), and approximations of others (the results that do require demographics)".

What that means for a reproduction can be stated exactly. Every comparison between groups of names reproduces from the public file, which is why Task 3 recovers the χ^2^ of analyst 8PTRZ to the third decimal. The model of the paper with community covariates does not. Refitted on the thirds, it gives z = −3.47 and a gap of −18.4 points, against the published z = −3.73 and −20.0 points. The difference is approximate by design and has a documented cause, so a reproduction that finds it has learned something about the file and nothing against the paper. The public file also holds 1,014 emails where the paper reports 1,017, and 14 of them carry no community thirds. The [codebook of the course file](../cases/housing/data/housing_audit_codebook.md) records each of these features of the data.

**The verification note.** The record carries a note: "This dataset underwent an independent verification process that replicated the tables and figures in the primary article. For the supplementary materials, verification was performed solely for the successful execution of code." The verification was carried out by the Odum Institute at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and the article was awarded the Open Materials badge of COS. The note does not say on which data file the verification ran, and the identifiable file was never public, so the note and the ReadMe are best read together: the tables and figures were verified, and a reader with the public file can reproduce the experimental results exactly and the models with covariates approximately.

**How the course uses it.** The repository of this site keeps four of the six files in `data-raw/housing/`, the identifiable do-file and its codebook not being needed, and the first script of the pipeline writes the two CSV files of the course from them: `audit_original.csv`, the public file with the column names of the OAs, and `housing_audit.csv`, the course file with readable names. Both are described column by column in their codebooks, and both ship with the workspace.

## 5. Versions of a record {#sec-versions}

A deposit changes after it is made, and a good repository keeps every state of it. The four repositories that the course meets do this in different ways.

**Dataverse** numbers the versions of a dataset. A change to the files makes a new major version (2.0), and a change to the metadata alone makes a minor one (1.1). The package of the OAs has two versions. Version 1.0 was published on 17 February 2016, when the article was still forthcoming, and its record gave the volume of the journal as 'Forthcoming'. Version 1.1 followed on 23 April 2017 and completed the citation with volume 61, issue 1 and pages 100–116; the six files are byte for byte the same in both, as their checksums show. The DOI resolves to the latest version, the Versions tab of the record lists them all with what changed, and a data citation names the version that it used. The citation of a Dataverse dataset also carries a **UNF**, a checksum that Dataverse computes from the values in the data rather than from the bytes of the file, so that the same data saved in another format give the same UNF.

**The OSF** keeps the versions of each file. Uploading a file under the name of one that is already there replaces it, but "a downloadable copy of the replaced file will be saved as a version", listed with its date under the Revisions tab of the file ([help.osf.io](https://help.osf.io/article/387-files)). The files of a registration cannot be changed at all once it is submitted.

**Zenodo** gives every version of a record its own DOI and adds a concept DOI that always points at the latest one. A paper should cite the version DOI, so that its readers get the version that it used.

**Git** records every commit, as the [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd) explains, but a repository on a forge can still be rewritten or deleted by its owner, which is why a release is archived on Zenodo before it is cited.

## 6. The SCORE dossier of the housing-audit case {#sec-trail}

SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence, put claims from published social and behavioural research through reproduction, robustness checks and replication [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. Each paper that it selected has a project on the OSF, named by a code that combines the first author, the journal, the year and a short identifier. The project of this paper is [osf.io/3a8bg](https://osf.io/3a8bg/), "SCORE - Einstein_AmJourPoliSci_2017_mxyQ", and it holds five components, one for each kind of material.

| Component | What it holds | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| [`nrt4s`](https://osf.io/nrt4s/) | The original materials of the paper, collected by the Center for Open Science | – |
| [`kcsby`](https://osf.io/kcsby/) | The power analysis for the replication | A target of 90% power to detect 75% of the original effect |
| [`9wp8d`](https://osf.io/9wp8d/) | The reproduction with the data and code of the OAs | An unfilled template; no reproduction outcome exists, and the Multi100 record marks the reproduction as never attempted |
| [`2ug8x`](https://osf.io/2ug8x/) | The replication with new data: the preregistration, uploaded on 5 May 2020, the final report, uploaded on 7 October 2020, and six sub-components (materials for the ethics review, methods and materials, data, analysis, power, and an audit of the replication) | **Not replicated**: no difference in greetings by name, z = 0.66, p = 0.511 on a random draw of 738 replies |
| [`38rsh`](https://osf.io/38rsh/) | Multi100, with one sub-component for each of the five analysts | Three analysts read their results as evidence for the claim and two as evidence neither for nor against it |

The replication also has a registration of its own, [osf.io/v6wd8](https://osf.io/v6wd8/), "Replication of a Research Claim from Einstein & Glick (2017), from The American Journal of Political Science". It was registered on 14 May 2020 with the OSF Preregistration template, kept under an embargo until 13 May 2024, and carries the DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/V6WD8. The embargo kept the plan private while the replication ran and the results were reported, and the date of registration, which the embargo did not change, still shows that the plan came first. The final report lists the ways in which the analysis departed from the plan, among them a logistic regression with covariates and the exclusion of county-level housing authorities, both added to match the model of the paper. The replication emailed 3,050 housing authorities, and the Data sub-component of its project, [osf.io/xseqg](https://osf.io/xseqg/), holds a deidentified data file, uploaded on 27 September 2020, with a do-file that runs the analysis without the identifying variables and a dictionary of the variables. A reader of the record can therefore check the plan against the report and has the data and the code with which to run the analysis again.

That table is what a well-kept record lets a reader establish without emailing anyone: a reproduction that SCORE planned and never carried out, a robustness study in which five analysts reached two different verdicts, although every statistic that Multi100 recorded comes from a gap in the same direction, and a replication with new data that found no difference, with its plan registered before its results. Each of those statements can be checked, because the materials sit in a public tree with dates on every file. The [case study](../cases/housing/index.qmd#sec-score) sets the same record in the story of the paper.

Four of the five analysts left their code, and the course reproduces all four statistics that Multi100 recorded from the public file. The scripts are read on the OSF, and the course does not copy them, since they belong to their authors and the OSF is where they are kept with their dates.

## 7. The SCORE dossier of the EU-frames case {#sec-trail-eu-frames}

Three nodes in the OSF tree contain the materials of the EU-frames case, and all three are public projects, which means that from 19 February 2027 they are read-only records at the same addresses (section 8).

**[`osf.io/8rtwe`](https://osf.io/8rtwe/) – the official Multi100 archival record.** The component that the Multi100 project preserved for analyst C6HJR: the materials as submitted, frozen and citable. The transition changes nothing about it, since it was already an archive in the strict sense.

**[`osf.io/6zqct`](https://osf.io/6zqct/) – the analyst's maintained fork, from which the course fetches its data.** OSF describes this node as "a public fork" of `8rtwe`, maintained by the facilitator for teaching. It contains a later revision of the analysis script and its exported dataset, revised Task 1 and Task 2 documents, and `EUframes_cy.csv` in its main folder, which is the file fetched by `R/get_data.R` in the workspace of the case. After February 2027 it can no longer accept a new file, so the maintained copy of the workspace from then on is the [`replication-lab`](https://github.com/CodeMoreh/replication-lab) repository on GitHub, whose releases are the versions to cite, and the fork on OSF stands as the record of the materials up to that date.

**[`osf.io/h7432`](https://osf.io/h7432/) – the full SCORE dossier, one paper put through all three Rs (reproducibility, robustness and replicability).** The parent node that contains every reproducibility check made on the case, with one component per check.

| Component | What | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `whp4b` | Original materials collected by the Center for Open Science | View-only |
| `cf8en` | Author-provided code – two Stata do-files, supplied on request; a statement by the original author (OA) records that the data cannot be forwarded and must come from GESIS | Code available, data restricted |
| `8fwrt` | Power analysis for the replication | – |
| `ezhcs` | **Push-button reproduction**, run with OA's own code | **Failed.** "The authors used file names that did not correspond with the names of the files available for download. Additionally 16 datasets are listed on the website as being used but the code references 18 files." |
| `4rjbf` | **Source-data reproduction** | **'Not reproduced'** – the effect size "could not be extract[ed] nor re-calculate[d]" from the source data |
| `gr8u6` | **Multi100 robustness** – five independent reanalysts, including analyst C6HJR whose materials this course reanalyses | All five coefficients negative; partial r as recorded from −0.006 to −0.452 |
| `zt5y2` | **Secondary-data replication** – later Eurobarometer waves, preregistered | **Not successful.** First report: b = +0.002, p = .046, N = 352,114; revised report of October 2026: b = +0.001, SE 0.0007, t = 1.428, p = 0.153, N = 331,668 |

That table is what a well-kept repository record lets a reader establish without emailing anyone: a push-button check that failed for a checkable reason, file names that did not match the files; a source-data check on which the reported effect could not be recovered; a robustness check that held the direction while the recorded size moved by a factor of nearly 80, most of it through the way in which the statistics were converted; and a replication on later data that was judged not successful, with both of its reports kept in the record. Each verdict can be checked because the materials are in a public tree, and the read-only status that the tree acquires in 2027 leaves that unchanged. Read-only status does mean that a project that is still being revised, as this course is, needs a working copy elsewhere, with the frozen record pointing to it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Open [`osf.io/h7432`](https://osf.io/h7432/) and find the `zt5y2` component in the table above. Locate the two reports of the replication in the materials of that component, the first and the revised one, and note for each the date on which it was uploaded and the coefficient that it reports, with its standard error and significance level. This is the kind of search that the OSF segment of Part 4 sets. After February 2027 the page will look the same, but nobody will be able to add to it.
:::

### 7.1 A map of the dossier {#sec-trail-map}

@fig-dossier draws the same dossier as a diagram, with one panel for each kind of material: the original materials collected by the Center for Open Science, the two reproductions, the five Multi100 components together with the fork kept by analyst C6HJR, and the replication on later waves with its preregistration. Projects and components, which can still receive files until the OSF makes them read-only in February 2027, are drawn differently from registrations, which are frozen from the moment they are made, and every box links to its OSF page when the diagram is [opened at full size](../assets/diagrams/score-teney-osf.svg). ### 7.2 Forks and archives {#sec-forks-archives}

A **fork**, in the git sense that the [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd#sec-github) uses, is your own editable copy of someone else's repository, kept separate so that you can change it without touching the original. The OSF had the same operation for projects, and "a public fork" is what OSF calls `osf.io/6zqct`. After 19 February 2027 no new fork can be made on the OSF, so forking remains available only on the code forges.

An **archive** freezes materials and a **registration** (section 9) freezes a plan, and the difference is what allows the date of a plan to be compared with the date of a result. The archival record at `8rtwe` and the Multi100 protocol are the two halves of that comparison for the EU-frames case, as the registration of the replication and its final report are for the housing-audit case.

## 8. The OSF after 2026 {#sec-osf}

The OSF, run by the non-profit Center for Open Science (COS), has been the general-purpose repository behind almost all of the materials used in this course. Its help pages describe an OSF **project** as "[a flexible, collaborative workspace where researchers can plan, manage, and share any part of their research lifecycle](https://help.osf.io/article/253-project-structure)", and a **component** as an "[optional sub-project nested within a parent project ... used to break a large project into smaller parts](https://help.osf.io/article/253-project-structure)". Projects and components form a tree. Each node has files, a wiki, a list of contributors, storage add-ons that connect to Google Drive or Dropbox or GitHub, and its own privacy setting, and a project can be forked, registered, given a DOI and linked to a preprint. That is the OSF that the literature of the last decade refers to, and that the records of both cases were built on.

### 8.1 The transition {#sec-transition}

On 27 August 2026 COS announced that OSF Projects are being phased out, and the help pages set out the timetable. The reason given is financial: keeping the projects workflow running "would require COS to raise approximately $4-5 million each year for the next several years", which the organisation cannot sustain, so the OSF is being narrowed to the parts where it can do most. Two dates matter.

- **From 16 November 2026**, "no new projects or child components of existing projects can be created on OSF. All other functions remain the same." Existing projects can still be edited, files added, contributors changed, until the second date.
- **From 19 February 2027**, "all OSF projects will be converted into a read-only project." Content stays viewable and downloadable at the same URLs and DOIs, an administrator can still delete a project or make a private one public, but nothing can be edited, added or uploaded, no new component or fork can be made, and a public project cannot be made private again. Private projects stay available to the people who already have access, and COS says it will give at least twelve months' notice before removing any of them.

For the two cases, nothing is lost. The SCORE project of the housing-audit paper and its components, and the three nodes of the EU-frames case, are public projects, so from February 2027 they are read-only records at the same addresses, and the registration of the housing-audit replication is unaffected.

COS also states that "Registrations & Preregistrations and Preprints are unaffected by this change". Both workflows continue, new registrations can be created, and the community-run preprint servers hosted on OSF Preprints keep running (the generalist OSF Preprints server itself has been closed to new submissions since 25 August 2025, with the existing preprints kept). Public projects remain "accessible indefinitely as read-only records", their DOIs "continue to resolve indefinitely", and OSF Search still finds them. COS summarises what the OSF becomes as "a free, open-source platform for creating and linking transparent research records", built around registrations, preprints and links to outputs held elsewhere. The FAQs add that the registration and preprint workflows "are not meant as replacements for Project storage", and that "Registrations are designed to document and share preregistrations, study plans, and similar practices. You should identify a data repository for sharing data, materials, and other supplements."

For someone with an existing project, the guidance is to do nothing if the project is a finished public record: "If your public Project does not need further updates, we strongly recommend that you take no action", because moving a deposit that already has a DOI risks a second DOI for the same work and a split citation record. An active project should be moved to a repository suited to its content before February 2027, with the OSF DOI or URL redirected to the new home through the [redirect request](https://help.osf.io/article/750-redirect-my-doi-or-url), which only an administrator of the project can submit. A private project should be exported or made public. The COS guide on [replicating a project structure](https://help.osf.io/article/749-replicate-your-project-structure-in-other-repositories) maps the OSF tree onto the alternatives: on Zenodo, one record for the former top-level project and one for each substantive component, linked through the "Related works" fields as parts of a whole; on Dataverse, a collection for the project with a child collection for each component and a dataset for each folder.

### 8.2 Working on the OSF from 2027 {#sec-osf-2027}

For a new piece of work, the **registration** is the record: a frozen, time-stamped document of the plan, created directly on OSF Registries without a project behind it, using one of the templates (the standard OSF Preregistration, the AsPredicted form, the secondary-data template and a dozen others), kept private under an embargo of up to four years if need be, and given a DOI the moment it is public. Files can be uploaded as part of the submission, within a 5 GB limit, but the data are not meant to be kept there. The data, the code and the materials go to a repository of the kinds described above, and their DOIs are entered in the **Resources** fields of the registration, which is also what earns a registration its open-practice badges for data, code and materials. A **preprint** on one of the community servers can point at the same DOIs. The OSF then holds the plan and the links while the deposits are elsewhere, which is the use that registrations were designed for and, after the transition, the only arrangement that the OSF offers for a new piece of work.

## 9. Registrations and preregistration templates {#sec-prereg-templates}

A **registration** is "[a frozen version of your project that can never be edited or deleted, but you can issue a withdrawal of it later](https://help.osf.io/article/330-registrations)", time-stamped and given its own permanent identifier. It is the mechanism behind preregistration: it records a study plan before the data are collected or, for a reanalysis of existing data, before the specific analytical choices are made, so that the plan cannot later be rewritten to fit the result. A public registration receives a DOI, and an embargoed one stays private for up to four years, as the registration of the SCORE replication of the housing-audit case did. [A registration can be updated through a transparent update that records what changed and why, and it can be withdrawn, which removes its contents but keeps the metadata and the justification. The Multi100 reanalysts worked from a registered protocol of this kind, which is why their results can be compared on equal footing.]{#sec-registration} What varies between registrations is the **template**, the fixed set of questions that a researcher answers before the analysis is run. OSF Registries hosts more than a dozen, and two of them matter for this course.

**The AsPredicted form.** Built by the team behind [AsPredicted.org](https://aspredicted.org/) and offered on the OSF as the "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org", it asks eight short questions, each answered in a sentence or two: whether any data have been collected, the main question or hypothesis, the dependent variable, the conditions, the analyses, outliers and exclusions, the sample size, and anything else worth recording. The preregistration block of Task 5 is modelled on it. Its brevity suits a course, since someone who has never preregistered can complete it in the time that the exercise allows, and what it demands is what a longer template demands: the analysis is stated before it is run, specifically enough that it cannot be reinterpreted afterwards.

**The template for secondary data.** A template written for a study whose data have not yet been collected assumes that the researcher has not looked at them, which is never true of a reanalysis. The template that van den Akker and colleagues wrote for the analysis of existing data asks instead what you already know: which parts of the data or of their published results you have read, whether your hypothesis was formed before or after that, and what was still open about your analytical choices when you wrote the plan. For a reanalysis of the kind that Multi100 commissioned, this is the more accurate statement of what a preregistration can promise. It cannot promise that you approached the data blind, only that your specific choices were fixed and dated before you ran them.

**How the block of the course maps onto these.** The block that you complete in Task 5 has the shape of the AsPredicted form, adapted for a reanalysis with a specification menu. Instead of a hypothesis and a test, it asks you to state the claim, one option on each of the eleven decisions of the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd) across Levels 1, 2 and 3, and a sentence, grounded in the causal graph of Task 2, on why that specification answers the claim. In the EU-frames case the block asks for one option on each of the fourteen decisions of its [specification menu](../cases/eu-frames/menu.qmd). Its second field, on the data and what you already know about them, stands in for the section on prior knowledge of the template for secondary data, which the AsPredicted form leaves out.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Read the question list of the AsPredicted template at [aspredicted.org](https://aspredicted.org/) and, separately, skim the structure of the secondary-data template. For a single specification that you might choose from the specification menu of your case – in the [housing-audit menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd), say, every delivered email, Hispanic against white names and a linear probability model without covariates; in the [EU-frames menu](../cases/eu-frames/menu.qmd), the positive composite as outcome, the raw unemployment rate, two-way fixed effects, all years and no weights – write one sentence answering the central question of the secondary-data template in your own words: what, if anything, had you already seen of the results on this claim before settling on that specification? A preregistration constrains your analysis only when that answer is truthful and the plan that contains it is dated before the specification is run.
:::

## 11. Depositing a reanalysis of your own {#sec-deposit}

Put together, the sections above give a route for depositing a reanalysis like the one that you build in the course, written so that it works after the OSF transition as well as before it.

1. **The code goes on a forge.** Put the report, the scripts and the codebooks in a git repository on GitHub or an equivalent, with a licence file and a README that says what the repository is and how to render it. The [git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd) takes you from nothing to that point.
2. **Each version is archived with a DOI.** Tag a release on the forge and let Zenodo archive it, so that the version you cite in a paper is the version that a reader gets.
3. **The data go where their licence allows.** Data released under CC0, such as the housing-audit data, can travel with the code, with a citation of the Dataverse record and its version. Data under a licence that forbids redistribution, such as the Eurobarometer files of the EU-frames case, never leave your machine, and the README says how a reader obtains them from the archive, as the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) sets out for that case. Data that could identify a person or an organisation stay out of a public deposit whatever the licence says, as the blinding of the public file shows.
4. **The plan goes on the OSF.** Create the registration on OSF Registries before the analysis runs, with the AsPredicted form or the template for secondary data, and put the DOIs from steps 2 and 3 into its Resources fields. Keep any embargo short.
5. **The report is part of the release.** Render it to HTML or PDF and include the rendered file in the tagged release, so that the numbers that a reader is shown are the ones that the code produced on the day of the release.
6. **Cite the data properly.** Give the citation that the repository provides for each dataset, with its version and the date of download, in the report and in the metadata of the deposit.

A reanalysis deposited that way has a public plan with a date, a public record of the code and the results with a version, and a stated route to any data that it cannot include. The record of the housing-audit case has nearly all of that, which is what made the exercise of the course possible without writing to anyone.
